title: Opposed to Proposed Rezoning
author: Lilli Tibbet
content:
Opposed to proposed rezoning

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 7 | Section: Letters

 I am a lifelong resident of Easton, Maryland. I am expressing my opposition to the proposed rezoning and development of the property at the end of Camac Street in Hunters Mill on Matthewstown Road.There are many in my community who share my concern, and I am writing on behalf of them as well.The development would cause traffic and safety problems, create even more problems with schools that are already over-capacity, destroy local wildlife habitat and potentially lower the property values of the existing community. I am asking for my community to reach out to our local government and protest the construction.Traffic and safety of pedestrians are major areas of concern. Traffic congestion between the intersection of Matthewstown Road (Rt.328) and Highway 50 and Mile Post Drive already makes driving this stretch of road hazardous. The addition of approximately 200 homes in the approved Gannon Estates and 120 apartments at the corner of Route 328 and Elliott Road will already increase the congestion and danger of the traffic patterns.Local neighborhood traffic will disproportionately surge during morning and evening rush hours, causing traffic issues during critical times for the existing area neighborhoods and commuters (including Hunters Mill, Matthewstown Run, Brentridge, Mulberry Station, Swann Haven and Caroline County commuters). The traffic surge during morning rush hours will also negatively impact the safety of children since students walk to the bus stop at the entrance of Hunters Mill.In general, the area traffic is continuing to increase, and heavy traffic is already common on Matthewstown Road.Schools in the area are already reported at over capacity, and the council should not approve multi-family dwellings that create or exacerbate this situation. Already approved housing developments in Talbot County will stretch public, private and parochial school admissions beyond capacity.Wildlife has been observed in the area and any development will destroy their habitat. Any planned development of the property should consider the continuing impact on local wildlife habitat.Within the project application, there are indications that the proposed planning area has several endangered species, which should be investigated by the appropriate agency before the approval of the project.Property values are likely to decrease in the area where multi-family apartments are built.Multi-family dwellings are inconsistent with the neighborhoods developed in this area.I am asking my community to attend meetings to speak out against the construction. title: Greensboro May Get Funds to Move Pump Station, Restore Site of Old Wastewater Treatment Plant
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Greensboro may get funds to move pump station, restore site of old wastewater treatment plant

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Though she wasn't on the agenda, Caroline County Assistant Director of Planning Leslie Grunden reported a positive development in protecting a stream flowing into the Choptank River north of Greensboro.Leading off the Jan. 23 meeting of the Caroline County Commission, Grunden said state funding was available to shore up "erosion at the town's pump station at the site of the old treatment plant located on a small tributary that feeds directly to the Choptank River," she said.
Greensboro Director of Public Works Brandon Cunningham alerted Commission President Travis Breeding about the "severe erosion" after recent significant rainfall.
"When he called me, and I went to look at it, I was like, 'Oh, yeah, this is a big deal,'" Breeding said.
Grunden said Cunningham told her he noticed "some erosion had been increasing" over the past several months.
"I think that was part of the old outfall for the old treatment plant, but the sides and the bottom are lined all the way down to the river — under the overpass into the river," Grunden said. "And over time, because it was probably put it in in the '60s, … it's broken up and starting to collapse and that's exacerbating the erosion."
A short-term solution in the form of an emergency grant was already in the works to add rocks and rebar and help hold the bank in place "while we went looking for funding for the long-term solution," to move the pump station farther uphill, Grunden said.
The aim is to remove the infrastructure and convert the stream location to a natural floodplain.
"Bringing the pump station up the hill (on town property) keeps it out of harm's way from erosion but also from eventual rising water from the Choptank," she said.
"This pump station takes flow from the town to the plant, so for that to be in jeopardy kind of keeps me up at night," Grunden said. The north county wastewater treatment plant is located on State Route 313, just north of Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company's community hall.
Grunden said her usual funding sources could support either the infrastructure or stream and floodplain restoration but not both. "So, I kind of put the word out saying we need money for both," she said.
However, the Maryland Department of the Environment gave her a call a week or two ago, "essentially (saying), 'We think we found the money to do both,' which is … almost a miracle," Grunden said.
MDE had "actually never done this grant. It's a grant they get from EPA that they've never had interest in," she said. "They would actually be the recipient, and then the county would be the sub-recipient. (MDE) would actually have to do all the reporting up to EPA, and I would provide them status reports and invoices."
She is currently putting together a project budget. Preliminary estimates put the pump station relocation at $1.3 million, and Grunden's guess is removing the structures would be half a million, with stream and floodplain restoration another half a million.
"And then I always have a contingency plan because nothing ever goes the way you want," she said. "So, we're at about $2.4 million. (The Department of Natural Resources) has reached out to say they'd be interested in helping with the stream and floodplain component, which would give us more money if we need more to deal with on the pump station side."
Grunden said she was "pretty confident" that enough funding would be available for the two-phase project, "where the first phase would be moving the pump station and demo-ing the old buildings, and the second phase would be going in and doing the stream and the floodplain restoration."
Although the project is "not a sure thing," she said MDE reaching out to her was "a really good sign that they're serious about providing the funding."
"I can't think of a better move that we can make there environmentally other than to get that stuff out of the floodplain," Breeding said.

title: Oxford Audit Brings Question of How to Strengthen Internal Controls in Small Town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford audit brings question of how to strengthen internal controls in small town

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — After a presentation on the Town of Oxford's fiscal year 2023 audit, commissioners received suggestions on how the town could address a material weakness for its segregation of duties.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, Roy Geiser, a partner at the accounting firm UHY, went through the highlights of the financial report. For fiscal year 2023, Oxford received an unmodified opinion, the highest level of assurance that can be given by an auditor.
"And what that means is (that) these financials as presented, in our opinion, are free of any material misstatements," Geiser said.
Toward the end of his presentation, Geiser detailed a material weakness that was found regarding the town's segregation of duties — meaning that there aren't enough town employees to separate financial duties.
"A lot of towns your size have this exact comment," Geiser said about the finding.
There are three levels of control deficiencies that auditors can find, Geiser said. These are: a deficiency, a significant deficiency or a material weakness.
Geiser said that material weakness is the most severe of these deficiencies. If found, a material weakness needs to be communicated by the auditor via a letter.
This is not the first year the Town of Oxford has received this comment about the lack of internal controls in its audit. According to the financial reports posted on the town website, this has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
Geiser suggested that commissioners ask questions if they ever notice something "out of line" when it comes to town finances.
After Geiser's presentation, Commissioner Katrina Greer asked him how other towns handle this material weakness issue.
Geiser said that while some towns don't do anything, others use a third-party consultant.
"They maybe bring them in quarterly just to have another set of eyes looking around," he said.
Some other towns, Geiser said, will have council member involved or set up an audit committee. He said an audit committee is "very rare" for a town the size of Oxford.
Greer said this is something the commissioners will be talking about more in the future.
At the previous town meeting on Jan. 11, Greer said she would like to discuss the possibility of hiring someone with a finance or accounting background to take on some of the town's financial duties in order to address this issue with internal controls.
"This would take some burden off the manager and enable us to comply with the audit recommendation of having multiple people performing financial roles," she said at the meeting.
Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said she had shared originally this idea with the commissioners because hiring more employees is the way to solve this problem.
"Admittedly most towns our size can't afford more staff," Lewis said at the Jan. 11 meeting. "Oxford is not in that situation, per se."
At the meeting Tuesday, one resident asked Geiser if hiring a part-time employee could solve the issue.
"In a perfect world, you want at least three people in your accounting function," Geiser said. "There are ways to get around it with other checks and balances. So a part-time person could help that situation."

title: Second Amendment Introduced for Lakeside Unit Resolution
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Second amendment introduced for Lakeside unit resolution

 January 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Environment 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A second amendment to previously introduced legislation relating to the number of equivalent dwelling units in each phase of development at Lakeside at Trappe was introduced Tuesday by two Talbot County Council members.The amendment, requested by council Vice President Pete Lesher and introduced by him and council member Lynn Mielke, would modify the still-pending Resolution 347 to incorporate provisions of separate, but related, Lakeside legislation — Resolution 338 and its amendment — into its language.
The original version of Resolution 347, first introduced last September, would amend the county's comprehensive plan to include the number of equivalent dwelling units for each phase of development at Lakeside, though the numbers for Phases 2 through 6 are estimated.
It also provides the current water and sewer classifications for each phase. A total of 2,874 equivalent dwelling units are planned at Lakeside.
The language to be incorporated from Resolution 338 proposes amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.
The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, only allowing for roughly 400 residential units to be built.
A major permit modification approved by the Maryland Department of the Environment is required for any future expansion of the wastewater treatment plant.
Resolution 338's provisions also would mandate any future expansion of the new plant to require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.
The resolution's amendment, introduced in November, adds language requiring a certification from the Talbot County Planning Commission of the amendment's consistency with the county's comprehensive plan.
At Tuesday's council meeting, Lesher emphasized that none of the language proposed to be added to Resolution 347 via its second amendment is new. It's a different way to help the county's Planning Commission come to a finding of consistency, he said.
Resolution 347, though considered in a multi-hour Planning Commission meeting last October, has yet to receive any final determination of consistency, which is required when amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
Multiple postponements of discussion on the legislation have lengthened the process, though the amended language of Resolution 338 was found consistent by the Planning Commission in December.
"This simply gives an alternative for the Planning Commission to say, 'Yes, with this language, if you combine it, we can find this consistent,'" Lesher said. "They may find Resolution 347 consistent without this amendment, they may find it consistent both without and with this amendment. If we get those alternatives, we then have that option to act at the council level."
The need for Resolution 347 stems from a request from the Maryland Department of the Environment last spring.
The agency asked the county to submit updated phase information and figures for water and sewer services with corrected classifications for all parcels within Trappe, including Lakeside, in a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.
Related legislation, Resolution 348, addresses the incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside under a draft discharge permit.
"Without that finding of consistency though, this resolution doesn't reach our desk," Lesher added, "and we don't have that way of bringing closure to the outstanding issues from MDE that will allow us to finish that Report of the Review."
Council Member Keasha Haythe questioned the need to add language from Resolution 338 into Resolution 347, saying the addition seemed to be the opposite of what the Maryland Department of the Environment requested.
The Town of Trappe is not on the same page as the county regarding the resolutions, she pointed out. Later, Haythe confirmed that the initial resolutions proposed were in line with what the agency wanted from the county.
The county's Planning Commission and the Public Works Advisory Board are set to discuss the two pending resolutions and amendments in a joint meeting on Wednesday, Feb. 7, at 11 a.m.
A public hearing on all three Lakeside resolutions and amendments will be held at 6:30 p.m. at the Tuesday, Feb. 13, County Council meeting.
Following Tuesday's meeting, council President Chuck Callahan issued a statement on the pending legislation.
"We understand that the resolutions regarding the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan and the Town of Trappe can be difficult to follow. It is a complicated matter with a lengthy history," he said in the statement. "The council looks forward to addressing this matter on Feb. 13, 2024, and resolving the concerns raised by the Maryland Department of the Environment."

title: CWDI and Dorchester County Council Not in Violation of Open Meetings Act
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI and Dorchester County Council not in violation of Open Meetings Act

 February 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Maryland's Open Meetings Compliance Board has found Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. and the Dorchester County Council not in violation of the state's Open Meetings Act for a Nov. 13 closed meeting held by CWDI.In its opinions delivered Feb. 1, the OMCB stated that CWDI was not in violation of the act because it is not a public body. It did not find the County Council in violation of the act because the council did not go into a "meeting" at the Packing House Nov. 13.
At the meeting, which brought together city and county officials and development consultants, CWDI justified going into closed session using two exceptions listed in the Maryland Open Meetings Act: "to consider a matter that concerns the proposal for a business to locate, expand, or remain" and "to discuss a matter where public discussion would adversely impact the public body's proposal process."
CWDI, a nonprofit that was formed by the City of Cambridge, Dorchester County and the State of Maryland, has been tasked with planning and developing space along the Cambridge waterfront, known as Cambridge Harbor.
Plans include public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said that during the meeting, CWDI talked about business deals it is working on.
Before CWDI entered into closed session on Nov. 13, WHCP reporter Jim Brady and Star Democrat Executive Editor Jim Johnson objected to the meeting being closed to the public.
Following the meeting, the Star Democrat and WHCP sent a complaint to the OMCB, alleging nine potential violations of the Open Meetings Act, including that the agenda topics were not consistent with the exceptions CWDI used to justify the closed meeting. The complaints were directed toward CWDI and the Dorchester County Council.
Although City of Cambridge staff and elected officials were also present at the November meeting, the Star Democrat and WHCP did not allege violations regarding the city's involvement in the meeting.
City Council voted against going into closed session at the Nov. 13 meeting, and one commissioner left so the city would avoid an Open Meetings Act violation.
OMCB OPINIONSAccording to the Feb. 1 opinions document, the OMCB found that CWDI didn't violate the Open Meetings Act because the non-profit is not a public body, and the act only applies to public bodies.
To determine whether CWDI could be considered a public body, the OMCB looked at how the entity was created and how its members were appointed to the board.
"As we have said before, '(p)erhaps the Maryland General Assembly might decide at some point to broaden the definition, so as to encompass all entities that carry out public functions,'" the opinions document says.
Leonard said he was not surprised by the decision made by the Compliance Board. He said it affirmed what CWDI "has said since it's beginning" — that it is a private corporation set to a public mission.
The reason CWDI listed the Open Meetings Act exceptions before going into closed session, he said, was to make CWDI's public partners feel comfortable.
"We list those exceptions, although we're not required to," Leonard said. "It's something we've done as a courtesy out of respect for our public partners since the beginning."
Brady, who objected to the Nov. 13 closed meeting, said it would be good for the state legislature to review what is considered a public body.
"I just find it unfortunate and unfathomable that an organization that's spending that kind of public money and ruling over that kind of land is not open to the public," he said.
The OMCB found that the Dorchester County Council didn't violate the Open Meetings Act because the Nov. 13 "gathering" wasn't a County Council meeting.
According to the opinions document, although all members of the council attended the gathering, the question was whether the Council "convened to consider or transact public business."
The OMCB said it could not conclude the gathering was a meeting based on the record presented.
"As we understand it, then, the Councilmembers attended the gathering to receive information, but the discussion was not a step in the Council's decision-making process regarding an item that was certain to come before the Council," the document says.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he was glad to see the decision that was made.
"There was never an intention for the Dorchester County Council to be violating any confidence of trust," he said.
In its opinions, the OMCB noted that "the appearance" of business being secretly conducted doesn't "serve the purpose" of the Open Meetings Act to "increase the faith of the public in government."
"Our conclusion in no way condones the action of a quorum of the (Councilmembers) in creating what was, at the least, an appearance of impropriety," the board said.

title: Approach is Obfuscation
author: Staff Writer
content:
Approach is obfuscation

 February 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 395
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I appreciate Mr. Schmidt's column that no more restrictions should be placed on Lakeside development. I am sure I am one of many that wondered why there is resistance to further reviewing Lakeside.There are at least three things questionable in Mr. Schmidt's column. First, he uses a form of dialogue that defies refutation. Namely, he throws out so many "facts" that refutation will take 20 times the space to address.
It would good if he addressed just one major issue. Let the entire column be about wastewater treatment or about traffic. If discussing wastewater treatment, address total capacity for wastewater treatment in Trappe and Talbot County. Instead, Mr. Schmidt jumps from wastewater to roads to the fire department to the new administration building, then ends his column by professing the infallibility of prior government action.
This approach is obfuscation. As Nietzsche said, "They muddy their waters that they may appear deep."
Second, it is hard not to notice that every good-deed dollar from the Lakeside developer goes to the town of Trappe. Money for the town police, for the town fire house, money to the Town Improvement Fund, and to the town new administration building. And he falsely claims that property taxes paid by the new residents will fund all the remaining requirements from Talbot County. It will not fund new school buildings and adding other essential services.
Last, Mr. Schmidt fails to address the ethics of "the tragedy of the commons." To put it in local terms, no matter what we do as an individual, we cannot destroy the entire Chesapeake Bay fishery. I can harvest crabs 24/7, and there will still be enough for others. But if everyone makes that same rational decision, there will be no crabs. The commons of the Chesapeake will be destroyed.
I think Mr. Schmidt is making a similar kind of argument by ignoring what would happen if every town did what Trappe has done. He is saying that since everything remains in Trappe – the people, the wastewater, the cars – then the commons of Talbot County has nothing to complain about. As one specific example, Mr. Schmidt states that Trappe will take care of all roads in Lakeside. Wonderful if those thousands of new cars never leave Lakeside roads. And all the thousands of residents never send their kids to Talbot schools.
His column did not support denying additional review.
MICHAEL DAVIS
Easton

title: National Vietnam War Veterans Day Observed in Chestertown
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
National Vietnam War Veterans Day observed in Chestertown

 April 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 CHESTERTOWN — On Good Friday, Memorial Park in downtown Chestertown filled with Vietnam War Veterans, their families and residents, to honor the veterans for their sacrifice.The March 29 event, Kent County's third National War Veteran's Day, saw a turnout of 240.
Veteran and organizer Peter Sweetser said 35 veterans stepped forward to receive their pin, a handshake and verbal affirmation, thanking them for their service.
As Sweetser put it, soldiers in Vietnam had a unique experience compared to other war veterans being that when they returned from their tour they were mistreated.
Alongside Sweetser, Kent County Commissioners Ron Fithian, Albert Nickerson and John Price proclaimed March 29 as Vietnam Veteran's Day.
They, as well as Chestertown Mayor David Foster, recognized Gold Star family members and spouses who lost veterans after the war.
Keynote speaker Larry Wilkerson, retired army colonel and chief of staff for former U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell, put forth examples of bravery in the conflict.
He not only used examples of American soldiers enduring the pain and loneliness war created. He used examples of the opposition as well, how in tearful, emotional movements both sides came together, bonding over losses suffered.
Wilkerson then talked about a soldier who fought bravely, not just in Vietnam but also against pancreatic cancer.
"That's the Vietnam War for me. So many Americans, so many brave men and women, and so much pain and agony, for what," he said.
All veterans who stepped up were anonymous, with the exception of Sfc. Samuel Tiller, age 95, who had received a Bronze Star and a Purple Heart for his bravery in Vietnam from April 12 to 14, 1964.
Sweetser, who noted that this is a private ceremony between the Department of Defense and the veterans, was pleased with the results.
"It was a great day of celebration for veterans who served nearly 50 years ago, supported by a large crowd of family, friends, and Kent and Queen Anne's County residents. Those men and women who answered the call to duty by their country, along with the MIA/POWs and the Gold Star families of that war and all wars, will never be forgotten," he said.

title: Local Legislators Reflect on General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Local legislators reflect on General Assembly

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Wednesday morning, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted a Legislative Wrap-up Breakfast with Maryland senators and delegates from the Eastern Shore.The meeting provided a summary and discussion of the recent Maryland state legislative session, the General Assembly. Topics discussed included DAF residual legislation and solar energy.
Sens. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) and Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), along with Dels. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), were in attendance.
Jacobs spoke on his work on the Environmental and Transportation Committee and the work both delegates and local leadership in Caroline County had on regulating dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals.
"I really do appreciate the fact that all three county commissioners and Caroline County were there because it had a huge impact on the committee in Annapolis," Jacobs said. "With an issue that meant that much to the county, all three county commissioners showed up and gave very compelling testimony as to the real problem."
DAF is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
House Bill 991 and its pair, Senate Bill 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County, who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery); Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation; and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation.
The bill is awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
SOLAR DEVELOPMENT
Delegates expressed concerns over legislation they said took away a vital part of the comprehensive solar development planning process, giving local communities less determination over solar expansion.
Jacobs spoke on Senate Bill 783, or the Brighter Tomorrow Act, which would lower the cost of developing Maryland solar projects and increase the value of solar energy for consumers across the state.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who was in attendance, argued that if counties are forced to have more solar, they should be able to negotiate and charge what they want from solar facilities. SB 783 attempted to limit taxes charged to commercial solar facilities.
"I made a comment in the committee: If solar was as good as we are told it's good … Why doesn't everybody in this room have it?" Arentz said. "We're pushing so hard for something we can do. And I think the General Assembly has to, at some point, wake up."
The state's Renewable Portfolio Standard had already established a nation-leading mandate to deploy solar that equals 14.5% of Maryland's electric demand by 2030. Maryland has fallen behind the pace to meet that goal, only meeting 55% of the policy's intermediate 2022 target.
After the delegates had reflected on this year's legislative session, Arentz expressed his appreciation to his fellow delegates for the work that was accomplished during the legislative session.

 Like many that the Star Democrat reaches, I hope, I look forward to locals expressing their (political) views with others in our wonderful community, which stretches beyond the boundaries of Talbot County.Recently we have had opportunities to read opinion pieces from both Republicans and Democrats regarding the merits of their party's representatives and the failings of representatives of the opposite party. Both have attempted to bolster their claims with the words of other partisans, or with (partisan) experts, or with "studies," which are, all too often, less than objective.
In that regard, many actually fail an objective smell test.
So, what is a voter to do, you ask. My advise, should you choose to listen, is to listen to both, no all, sides, if possible. There are likely kernels of truth in things they say, emphasis on kernels. However, kernels do not the whole cob make.
Be skeptical of partisans, they likely have agendas that may not serve the interests of communities at large well. Why is that important, you ask. After all, don't we want the kind of government that best serves our own personal interests and of those with similar interests? Isn't that what political parties are all about? Perhaps, but I would argue, that should not be what they should be all about.
As a member of the post World War II baby boomer generation I grew up during a period of time when fathers worked and mothers stayed home to nurtured the family. When neighbors talked to one another, took care of one another and gave consideration of how what they did would affect others in their communities. That is more difficult now, for any number of reasons, but do we really want to walk away from community responsibilities? Is that in our own best interests? I would argue, no.
Why is that? Because, in my opinion, we all do better, when we all do better. Life and communities are not zero sum games. There are prices to be paid when we do better, at the expense of others. It's basic civics.

 OXFORD — In an effort to rebuild from controversy faced in the aftermath of a recent hire, Oxford hosted a public comment and passed a resolution to better vet future candidates.With the anticipated large turnout for the Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, the town opted to move the event from its regular location on Market Street to the Oxford Community Center.
More than 100 people were in attendance, with many people standing against the walls of the building when available seating was filled.
"This has been a difficult and frustrating period for our town and its leadership," Commissioner Tom Costigan said to the crowd. "... We thought we had secured the services of the best candidate possible using the information we had available. I'm disappointed to admit that we were wrong."
CONTROVERSEY
The center of controversy is Michael Calvert, the town's would-be-town manager.
Calvert — who was previously a city administrator for Liberty, South Carolina — had been slated to get sworn in as Oxford's next town manager at this meeting. But just three days after announcing the hire, the Commissioners of Oxford announced the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
According to a statement sent out June 27, the town and Calvert determined that "it was not a good fit."
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some community members expressed concerns. Oxford resident Scott Rensberger said it was "shocking" the town didn't vet Calvert more because it took him a short time to find out "there were a lot of problems" in Liberty.
Former Liberty City Council member Peggy Edwards told the Star Democrat she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
According to a November news release from the City of Liberty, Calvert resigned at the beginning of the year after nearly two and a half years in the position. He cited family relocation as the reason for his resignation.
MOVING FORWARD
Commissioner Katrina Greer said Tuesday it was essential to move forward with the hiring process methodically, thoughtfully and with more input.
"I move to make a resolution to have a search firm conduct the search for a town manager," Greer said. "... This process of finding the right firm and the right fit might take several weeks, and we will be looking for input, but we should tell the public that we have a plan that we are going to professional services."
Greer said this resolution would require the town to use a "professional search team that specializes in local government." Costigan seconded the resolution, and it was unanimously approved by the commission.
In March, the commissioners voted to place advertisements for Lewis' position and issue a request for proposal for a search firm in the event it is needed. On June 27, Costigan said the town did not end up using a search firm in the search that resulted in Calvert's hire.
In addition to the resolution, Greer said the town should not delay too long in moving forward with hiring a new candidate due to the pressure it would put on the staff.
PUBLIC COMMENT
During public comment, several people spoke their concerns to the commission.
Jane Greenhawk, an Oxford resident, said she appreciated that the town will be using a professional search firm but would like answers to how the town ended up in this position in the first place. She asked several questions of the commissioners, including whether or not a criminal background check was completed and who had completed the background check?
Lyndsey Ryan, Oxford Attorney, attempted to answer all of Greenhawk's questions. After a bit of back-and-forth, Ryan said the background investigation was done through an online firm by the prior town manager.
In a June 28 statement, the Commissioners of Oxford said that Calvert underwent a pre-employment background check but that the results could not be disclosed because they are "confidential personnel records."
Grace Nave, an Oxford native, advocated for hiring someone local to fill the position.
"I really am so proud of this town that I know there's a lot of hiccups in it," Nave said. "There's good, bad, ugly and sad, but I want us to try to maybe think about the possibility of hiring someone local. If you hire somebody professional, you might get the top notch, but if they're out of town, they don't love this town like we do."

title: Tangier Ferry Captain Retiring

 TANGIER, Va. — Townfolk came out to thank Capt. Mark Haynie, who is retiring after ferrying thousands of tourists between the Maryland Eastern Shore and Tangier Island for the past 15 years.July 19, the Tangier Volunteer Fire Department used a hose to spray water high in the air over Haynie's boat, Sharon Kay III, as it motored toward the town dock where a crowd awaited to congratulate the good captain for his service.
Mayor James "Ooker" Eskridge gave a short speech to mark the occasion of Haynie's last run to Tangier.
"Mark would always be willing to add special and emergency medical charters. At any time, day or night, Mark could be counted on, even in the dead of night, hauled out of bed for a medical emergency. Tonight marks his last official regular run. Fair winds are following seas as you enter retirement, Captain. Your rest is well earned and deserved. You will be sorely missed."
With a skilled hand behind the wheel, Haynie is comfortable piloting the Sharon Kay III, which holds up to 29 passengers, as he ferries tourists back and forth seven days a week across the Tangier Sound between the island where he grew up and Crisfield, Maryland.
"Yeah. I'm going to miss it," said Haynie, a native of Tangier Island. "I'll miss talking to people and dealing with people. I'm going to miss it."
Being a waterman comes naturally to Haynie, 71, who spent a lifetime crabbing and oystering on the Chesapeake Bay before turning his wheel toward the ferry service in 2008. The trip between the island and Crisfield takes about 45 minutes where folks can see Smith Island, Maryland, and other barrier islands.
Approaching Tangier, tourists revel at the iconic Swain Memorial Methodist Church or the water tower in the distance as the boat approaches the crab shanties bordering the harbor.
"The trip is pretty easy most of the time," Haynie said. "Most times, the weather's pretty good. Winter time, you have some bad trips. But yeah, I've enjoyed almost every minute of it."
Cruising the Chesapeake Bay can be a pleasant experience with smooth waters or a bit more animated crossing because strong winds and bad weather mean steering through rough waves.
"Well, we had one time that we had a funeral," Haynie said. "... Like when we got in Crisfield we had 60-65 mph winds, so that was too dangerous to be out in, but that hit us while we're out there. We made it in with 23 people."
A skilled waterman, Allen Parks, is taking over Haynie's route to bring tourists to Tangier and make other important runs as needed 12-13 miles away to Crisfield, Haynie said.
So what's next for Haynie? He's too skilled as a captain to sit on the dock of the bay wasting time as the Otis Redding song says.
"Well, I'd like to find something to do. I got a smaller boat. I could travel around in her and all. There's some fishing and crabbing, fishing," Haynie said.

title: Urban Design Consultant Presents Analysis of Easton's Economic Potency

 EASTON — Town employees and representatives gathered at the Easton Town Office on Aug. 22 for a presentation of Easton's economic potency for land use planning.Joe Minicozzi, the principal and founder of Urban3, an urban finance consulting group, spoke during the presentation regarding Easton's potential to up its economic potency. He compared the growth of the town to the trajectory of one's DNA.
"Cities all have those moments," Minicozzi said. "They all have a DNA baked into them through their infrastructure, their growth patterns, that will have effects into the future."
Miguel Salinas, the town's director of planning and zoning, helped organize the partnership with Urban3 and last week's presentation.
"We hired Urban3 to model the potential revenue implications of various development scenarios based on different types of land use, … how we build out, … and at what densities," Salinas said.
Minicozzi pointed out the success of Easton's core downtown area. His presentation provided hypothetical examples of how much certain residential developments, businesses and homes could deliver in property taxes per acre.
"As Talbot County taxpayers, you take up 3% of the county's footprint, you're producing 26% of the county's property taxes," Minicozzi said of the town. He encouraged the town to find "opportunities for infill" and "neighborhood growth areas."
Urban3's analysis noted there was a potential $637,000 in property tax revenue from a Poplar Hill housing proposal that never came to fruition.
In August 2023, an application from a developer to build 456 residential units between Easton Bypass and Oxford Road was rescinded. A 119-unit plan was approved by the Easton Planning Commission in September 2023, but this February, Talbot County bought the 120-acre Poplar Hill Farm property.
"That was an opportunity lost," Minicozzi said. "Make sure that you account for that or find a way to learn from this and do it in another place. Maybe that's not the right place, that's cool, your decision. But don't just avoid that."
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who attended the meeting, said he felt it was "inappropriate" for the presentation to mention the canceled Poplar Hill proposal given that it was a "democratically led and made decision."
"The data are perfectly useful in their own way," Montgomery said of the presentation as a whole, "but I was disturbed by the way the presentation made it seem like the only objective we should have … is how we can maximize the amount of tax revenue we can take in. And that's just wrong. There are so many other things that matter, starting with how we preserve the character of the town and maintain our rural character, maintain our open spaces."
During the presentation, Minicozzi raised the topic of sea level rise. He noted Maryland Department of Planning projections that predict Talbot County will lose $817 million in property value due to sea level rise by the year 2100, with $8.1 million of that coming in Easton.
Minicozzi also encouraged the town to ensure underrepresented groups of people — such as those under 45 and the town's non-white population — should be heard in conversations of economic potency.
"Those folks get pushed out of the community and take on more burden in transportation to get here," Minicozzi said, "which is even more painful financially."
Salinas said the analysis and presentation brought information that can serve the town's planning and zoning department moving forward.
"This information can be important for us to add another tool to the toolbox," Salinas said.

Leaders of Chesapeake Community Development, the developer for the project, have made a point to work with local community members on the overall outcome of the development.
According to Ross Benincasa, vice president of Chesapeake Community Development, Wednesday's meeting showed attendees the initial site plan. Chris Wheedleton, consultant at Rivers and Roads, was hired on the project to lead in gathering feedback from the community. Wheedleton said the meeting provided a chance to answer any questions residents might still still have regarding the new site.
After a presentation of the site plan, people were separated into groups and were encouraged to answer two questions: "Would you like what you saw?" and "What would you like to see differently moving forward?"

 In the 2020 election, Talbot County's outcome was decided by just 116 votes out of over 22,000 cast. In communities like ours, your vote — your individual voice — carries significant weight.While much of the focus in this election cycle is naturally on the presidential and congressional races, Talbot County also has three important school board elections, several judicial candidates, and two critical ballot measures to consider.
In an election cycle flooded with misleading mailers and interference from a nationwide, Republican-leaning PAC attempting to sway the outcome, I encourage all voters to take a close, thoughtful look at each candidate and their positions.
Regardless of your party affiliation, it would serve us well to vote for the candidates who are the most curious and driven for common-sense solutions, the ones who are both passionate and compassionate. Vote for the people with experience and objective professionalism and vote as if the future of Talbot County depends on your voice. Because it does.
There are several convenient ways to cast your vote — by mail, early voting at the Easton Fire Hall or on Election Day itself. The key is to start by making your voting plan. Ask yourself: Am I registered to vote? Where and when should I vote? Do I need a ride, or can I bring a friend or family member along? Will I need time off work or child care arrangements? These are important considerations to address ahead of time, so you're not caught off guard by travel plans, a child's event, or a late work shift on Election Day. Voting has never been easier, more efficient, or more secure.
We have put together an informative and accessible resource page – TalbotDems.org/VOTE – that provides voter information links, election dates and candidate information. Even if you do not agree with our positions, you might find the information provided useful.
In the final days of this election, I hope we can take a moment to reflect upon and appreciate the incredible personal and professional sacrifices of our friends and neighbors managing our local elections and running for office. We should rise to their example and be active participants in the democratic process.
The first step toward coming back together as a nation is participating in the democracy that generations of Americans have fought for, marched for, sat in for and walked out for, cried and cheered for, and sacrificed and died for.

 CAMBRIDGE — In a 3-2 vote, the Dorchester County Council passed a bill that addresses setbacks and buffers, ownership, and decommissioning plans for accessory, small scale and utility scale solar energy systems.After the bill was passed at a meeting on Nov. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said this is a start for solar legislation in the county.
"Laws can be amended and modified," he said. "But if we don't do something now, before the start of the General Assembly, we could be facing much worse without any safeguards in place."
Council members Rob Kramer and William Nichols voted against the bill. Council member Ricky Travers, Council Vice President Mike Detmer and Pfeffer voted in favor of it.
Under the new bill, solar developments located off scenic byways will need to be set back 100 feet from all property lines, and developments that are not located off of scenic byways will need to be set back 75 feet. Requirements regarding vegetative buffers, perimeter fencing, topsoil and site plans are also in the legislation.
The bill defines who the owners of a solar site are. Pfeffer said in an interview with the Star Democrat in September that the owners of the property and the operator of the solar development would both be considered the owner.
The bill was reintroduced in September after getting tabled in March. In the reintroduced bill, a section was added regarding decommissioning solar projects. Per the legislation, a decommissioning plan will need to be submitted and approved by the county prior to the building permit application.
In the September interview, Pfeffer said the bill was tabled so the council could wait for state solar legislation to go into affect and make sure the county was in line with it.
At the meeting Nov. 4, residents thanked the council for their efforts and shared concerns that the county bill doesn't do enough to restrict solar development.
The reintroduced bill left out a section in the original proposed bill that put a cap on how many aggregate acres of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems.
Beth Hill said although she feels the bill is a step in the right direction, she thinks there needs to be a cap on the number of acres in the county that can be used for solar development.
"Other counties around us do have caps," she said, mentioning Caroline County, which has a 2,000-acre cap on total rural land available for solar development.
Tracy Whitby-Fairall, who attended a town hall on the subject that Detmer hosted the previous week, said she recognized the county's efforts. She called the bill a "good foundation for a strong framework" for the county.
"I think there are some things that could be improved," she said, later adding, "I hope this isn't the end of the legislation. I hope this is the beginning."
Erick Windsor, who asked the council to vote against the bill, talked about the county's history of thriving tomato, dairy and lumber industries, which are now gone. He said that large solar operations take land away from grain farming.
"And this is going to affect all the other industries in this county that work around grain farming, like chicken farming," he said. "So you hurt the chicken farmers and you're going to hurt the industry in Hurlock that processes all this stuff."
Windsor said more restrictions need to be put on solar so it doesn't "decimate" the north part of the county.
Detmer said the bill — especially the decommissioning component — is "crucial" to have at the county level before the Maryland General Assembly session begins in January. He talked about the possibility of additional legislation coming down from the state.
"The Wild West of solar that we are in right now, I'm very bothered by it," he said. "I think we have to plant our flag here in this place that we're ready to go right now. If we don't act tonight, the law's not going to be in place when the session starts."
Detmer said this isn't the end of creating legislation around solar, but action needs to be taken now.
"We've got to put the seatbelt on," he said.

title: Delaware College Town Could Lift Longtime Ban on Tattoo, Piercing Shops
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware college town could lift longtime ban on tattoo, piercing shops

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News

 Newark, Delaware's decades-long prohibition on tattoo and piercing shops may be coming to an end.A majority of city council members indicated earlier this month they would be in favor of allowing such businesses to open. A formal vote will be taken later.
The discussion was initiated by a request from Brittnie Lopez, the owner of B13 Tattoos, currently located on Miller Road in Wilmington.
After operating the shop for three years, Lopez wants to move it to Newark's Main Street, noting that many of her customers are down here. B13 Tattoos operates on an appointment-only basis, and Lopez is the only employee.
"As the City of Newark has continued to thrive and add new additions and create different opportunities, I think that this would be perfect for the center of Newark," Lopez told council members.
She is in negotiations to lease a vacant storefront at 170 E. Main St, the building that also houses Frolic, Oishii Sushi & Ramen and Occupy Studio.
"I recently found out you guys have no tattoo parlors in the City of Newark, and I would love to be first," Lopez said.
In order for her to do so, however, city council must add body art establishments — a term that encompasses both tattoo and piercing shops — to the zoning code. Currently, body art establishments are not listed as an allowable use in any of the zoning districts, meaning they are essentially banned from opening anywhere in city limits.
This is not the first time Newark has discussed legalizing body art establishments.
In 2016, a business owner wanted to open a piercing shop on Main Street, but he ultimately dropped his request before it came to city council for a vote.
The topic came up again in 2022 when councilmen Travis McDermott and Jason Lawhorn said they had heard from people who wanted to open tattoo shops in the city. Council directed staffers to research the issue, but it fell by the wayside amidst other priorities and was never formally considered.
Lawhorn said tattoos and the people who have them were once stereotyped, but he argued that times have changed.
"Maybe in the '50s or '60s, it seems like it was associated with biker clubs and prostitution and things like that," he said. "It has evolved well past that."
Lawhorn, who said he has four tattoos himself, cited statistics that show that more than 40 percent of adults under 50 have a tattoo.
Allowing tattoo shops will bring something new to downtown Newark, he said.
"I think it adds some flavor and some culture to the city," Lawhorn said. "We love our restaurants, but there's not a lot of grit to Main Street."
Councilwoman Dwendolyn Creecy noted that tattooing goes back centuries and is important in many cultures.
"I don't have a problem with this. Not one," Creecy said.
The only council members opposed were Corinth Ford and John Suchanec.
"I really don't think that this is a business that would be compatible or required on Main Street," Suchanec said. "I probably have to come up with 1,000 reasons why I'm taking this position, other than my personal preference not to have tattoo parlors on Main Street."
He also worried that University of Delaware students would upset their parents by getting tattoos.
"One big, big concern is students going home and showing off their tattoos," Suchanec said, speculating their parents would respond by saying, "you didn't ask my permission."
Ford said her concerns are about safety and sanitation.
"I really do not want this kind of business on Main Street," she said.
The planning department will now work on language to add body art establishments to the zoning code.
It's expected that the law will require a special-use permit, meaning that each business owner will need permission from city council to open a tattoo or piercing shop. The permit can be denied or revoked if council determines that the business would be a detriment to the community. The city is also considering requiring body art establishments to operate on an appointment-only basis to eliminate spur-of-the-moment tattoo decisions.
The planning commission will vote on the law Dec. 3, with a final vote by city council in February.

title: Talbot County Council Denies Raise in Accommodation Tax
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 879
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A controversial proposal to raise the accommodation tax was voted down by the the Talbot County Council Tuesday.During an impromptu public comment period, lodge owners and community members expressed concerns over the increase in the accommodation tax saying it would hurt profits and tourism in the county. Additional comments concerning a lack of information were shared resulting in the proposal not passing.
The rise of the accommodation tax was presented by Cassandra Vanhooser, director of the department of Economic Development and Tourism, on Tuesday who gave an overview of the steps taken by her department to get a proposal in front of the council including approval for the Tourism Board of Talbot County and receiving support from Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels and Trappe.
"(Talbot County Council is) being called on to balance the effects on tourism businesses with the benefits to the towns and the county," Vanhooser said. "The Tourism Board has weighed the evidence, and they believe that the benefits outweigh the disadvantages."
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels and short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Despite voting down an increase, the council voted to strengthen the existing accommodation tax.
Martha Sparks, financial director for Talbot County, suggested removing the 120-day grace period for owners of short-term rentals to provide accommodation tax collected to the county before the county can impose a 10% penalty. Sparks proposed that the council approve a request to the legislature to reduce that period of time.
The council unanimously approved the proposal.
Prior to voting on a letter of support for the accommodation tax increase, several people began to raise their hands in order to get their opinions on record. Commission President Chuck Callahan opened the floor for public comment.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment, business owner Scott Wagner expressed concern on raising taxes saying that though the accommodation tax has not been raised in 20 years, prices of rooms for rentals have, which in turn provides more funds from accommodation tax.
Wagner said room rates have "ridden the wave of inflation" and described raising the accommodation tax to "feeding the monster."
"This is feeding the monster, and the monster is asking for a million dollars more next year, so when the monster is going to get fatter. I've never seen the tax go down, quite frankly."
In contrast, Jessica Bellis, a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed concern over the negative connotation with the accommodation tax.
"We can use words like the monster that you're feeding, but the monster is making sure that we do have the roads and the infrastructure and the police department and the marketing to be able to promote and sustain tourism, which is a major industry in Talbot County," Bellis said.
Included in public comment were concerns over information. Kevin Hartmann, Easton resident, said lodging providers were not asked for comment at the time of the town's vote. He said the towns were "significantly under-educated as to the ramifications."
According to Hartmann, two surveys were conducted to gather the opinions of lodging operators. One was done by the Talbot County Tourism Board and the other was conducted by Hartmann. The board's survey, he said, showed 75% of operators did not support the increase in tax. For the survey done by Hartmann it was over 84%.
The survey by the tourism board was released on Dec. 5 and the last town to vote on supporting the raise was on Dec. 4.
"You have in your package, letters from your five towns of Talbot County, each one of those voted for the increase," Hartmann said. "But the significant difference is this: None of those towns heard what you're hearing tonight, none of those towns have the results of the survey at the time of their vote. None of those towns held a public hearing on the matter."
After hearing the comment given by Hartmann, Easton Council President Frank Gunsallus, spoke and shared his thoughts on the information provided.
"Our vote already occurred, but after hearing all the testimonies tonight, and especially Mr. Hartmann's … perhaps we could have been better educated before we voted," Gunsallus said. "I believe that people reserve the right to change their mind, and I know our votes were cast, but I am, on your record, withdrawing my support for this accommodation tax."
After much deliberation from the council, the motion was denied in a 3-2 vote with Councilmembers Pete Lesher and Keasha Haythe voting in support of the proposal.
Vanhooser, director of Economic Development and Tourism, said Wednesday that the proposal failed and will not move forward this state legislature period.
"The Tourism Board obviously supports this, because they see it as a way to fund my department and tourism marketing and promotion, and the towns, you know, were in favor, despite what was said last night, because it raises their revenue, which they need for the various things they spend the money on."

St. Michaels' staff reached out to other trash and recycle businesses for new bids but only Republic Services sent in a bid. Ultimately, the commissioners approved the three year contract with Republic Services.
TOWN MANAGER RECRUITMENTFinally, a bid was approved for the Mercer Group Associates as the firm to lead recruitment of the next Town Administrator.  CAMBRIDGE — Hours after a rally was held questioning Rep. Andy Harris' (R-Md. 1st) loyalty to his constituents, Harris told Dorchester Chamber of Commerce members inside the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina that his office is here to help them."We can make your business run easier," he said during his keynote speech for the chamber's 79th annual business meeting and dinner. "We can work through the bureaucracy. Please get in touch with my office. We're more than happy to help you."
Earlier that evening, protesters lined the sidewalks of U.S. Route 50 outside the Hyatt, calling on Harris to hold a town hall and questioning whether Harris' allegiance is to his constituents or to Elon Musk and the Trump administration. The rally was organized by Cambridge Indivisible, a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders.
Speaking to members of the media after the chamber dinner, Harris said he didn't believe many of the people at the rally were his constituents.
"They're brought in by buses," he said. "I don't know where those buses come from. And we know that the national Indivisibles are involved. So we believe that a lot of those people aren't even constituents."
Harris said he heard from a Washington, D.C., organization's leader "who knows what's going on" that people at the rally were getting paid to be there. He said he would not name who told him that.
"This is astroturf," he said. "This is not grassroots."
Cambridge Indivisible Founder and Chair Michelle Fowle said many of those at the rally were her neighbors who live in Cambridge.
"He's just a liar," she said about Harris.
Harris said he will be holding a virtual town hall on March 25 so he can communicate with constituents from all over his district.
"If these protesters want to call in, if they want to get on my town hall, I will answer that question on my town hall," he said. "But I'm not going to hold a town hall for 100 people when I could hold a town hall and reach out to 5,000 people who don't have to leave their homes, get bused in by some entity paying for that bus."
Harris said he is "laser focused" on working for his constituents and advancing the Trump administration's agenda.
"Who also won the district with high numbers," he said about President Donald Trump (R) getting elected in November.
In Dorchester County, Trump won 55.99% of the vote, according to the Maryland State Board of Elections.
During the rally before the chamber dinner, protesters brought up concerns with recent mass firings of federal workers. Suzanne Sullivan said she has concerns about what the firings will do for the local economy. Sullivan, who lives in Dorchester County, is the wife of environmental scientist Jake Shaner, who was recently fired from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Harris told media after the dinner that most companies layoff employees every three to five years. He said that with federal tax cuts, the federal government will grow the economy so there are "plenty of jobs for every American."
"Look, do I feel for everybody who's laid off?" he asked. "Absolutely. Private industry, public government. It's a personal family setback. That's exactly why we have unemployment insurance and we have the social net until these individuals find another job."
HARRIS' KEYNOTE SPEECH
During his keynote speech, Harris touched on a number of issues relevant to Dorchester County and the Eastern Shore. He spoke about the importance of the agriculture industry, low-cost energy and the H-2B visa program.
Harris also brought up the need for blue catfish processing centers to help reduce the population of the invasive species in the Chesapeake Bay. He said federal funding will be available to entrepreneurs who want to build processing plants so the catfish can be considered a commercially viable seafood product.
Harris said two things the county should focus on are addressing drug and alcohol addiction and making sure every child is reading on grade level.
"And we can certainly provide help from the federal government," he said. "But I'll tell you, some of the best solutions are at the local level."
Harris, who lives in Cambridge, said it is a pleasure to represent the people of the Eastern Shore. He said he lives a "blessed life" where he can be at Mar-a-Lago one night and eating at Cindy's Kitchen in Cambridge the next morning.
"It's like the best of both worlds," he said. "And to be honest with you, I like Cindy's better. But don't tell the president that."

 OXFORD — On June 17, the Town of Oxford will choose someone to fill one of three town commissioner seats. The race is between incumbent Tom Costigan and resident Dave Donovan. The winner will serve a three-year term.The Star Democrat sent a questionnaire to candidates running in the election to allow them to share their perspectives on various town issues in their own words.
Tom CostiganAge: 67.
Family: Married 39 years.
Occupation: Oxford Town Commissioner; retired realtor.
Political Experience: Three years as Oxford Town Commissioner.
Why are you running for office?
I am now, and have been for many years, dedicated to the town of Oxford. I devoted 12 years serving on our Historic District Commission (10 of those as chair) in the interest of preserving and protecting our architectural and cultural heritage. I've also spent countless hours volunteering within our community.
We're in the midst of progressing on many important challenges and projects, and I am determined to see them through. The institutional knowledge I've acquired in service to our town covers every facet of our government.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are to fully staff and equip our police department; attract, retain and support our town staff; complete Oxford's comprehensive plan (our road map to the future); continue our progress on flood and stormwater control (pumps and check valves); complete our infrastructure projects (water upgrades, shoreline protection); hold the line on property taxes and water/sewer fees; limit the growth trajectory of short-term rental properties; explore new technologies to defray escalating utility costs; support our local businesses and civic organizations and help them thrive; continue to resist Oxford Road development/sprawl; and ensure that Oxford's future is determined by full-time residents.
How should Oxford address the flooding and infrastructure concerns in the town?
We are addressing these issues. I have personally visited other coastal jurisdictions, where they shared their knowledge, challenges and solutions. Here in Oxford, we have successfully installed check valves and tide gates to limit tidal inundation in vulnerable areas. We have procured ARPA funding, which will allow us to purchase mobile pumps. I will continue to lobby the state government to resolve flooding issues at the Causeway (a choke point that can cut our town off from emergency services). In addition, I'll continue to seek new solutions such as cisterns to collect stormwater and appropriate plantings to further mitigate flooding.
How would you as an Oxford commissioner ease tensions between residents and the commission?
It all starts with effective communication. One recent example relates to our FY2025/26 budget planning, where we hosted citizen workshops to explain our financial projections and to garner the public's input. During my tenure, I've initiated live streaming of all town meetings. I instituted the Constant Contact platform to inform residents of helpful messages relating to meeting agendas, board openings, weather alerts, events, etc. In addition, we've implemented a new, more user-friendly website for ease of locating information. I will always welcome and respect new voices and ideas to enhance transparency.
What is your vision for the Strand Beach project?
Most importantly, I want to see the Strand project succeed. When the next major storm hits, I want to provide the most resilient protection possible. Did you know that the east end of the Strand was once an island? This project, which has been discussed in public workshops and presentations since 2010, is being done with grant funding, not costing local taxpayers a single dollar. As for the logs, discussions should continue as to their disposition — It's a question of aesthetics vs. ecological benefit. Bottom line: the project is working, the beach area is expanding and plantings are taking root.
Dave DonovanAge: 67 years old in June.
Family: I have been married to my wife Rose for 44 years this August. We have three children and two grandchildren.
Occupation: I retired at the end of 2018 from my partnership in a large law firm in Washington, D.C.
Political Experience: I have not previously sought to hold any public elective office or played any role in a political campaign other than as a low-level volunteer.
Why are you running for office?
For the past three years, the town has made needless mistakes that have created and exacerbated deep frustration among our residents. These errors include mishandling the termination of a long-time police chief; appointing a candidate to fill the balance of the term of a resigning commissioner rather than holding an election as the voters demanded; failing to manage completion of the Strand project; and utterly botching the hiring of the previous Town Manager last summer. We have serious issues that need to be addressed. I have the experience to help us make needed improvements, minimize damage already done and avoid repeating errors.
What are your priorities if elected?
We need to correct and complete the Strand project and get it behind us. Sound financial management is also a top priority. We need sensible management of our substantial cash reserves. I also will prioritize open and candid communications about all our issues, engaging the community to discuss potential solutions, and leveraging the incredible reservoir of talent and expertise we have in Oxford. We need to take advantage of the skills and experience of our residents and not shut them out, as has happened far too often in the last three years.
How should Oxford address the flooding and infrastructure concerns in the town?
We have had a plan in place for nine years to address flooding and infrastructure and done next to nothing to implement it. Addressing the Strand was the lowest priority in that plan, yet it has almost completely swallowed our attention. We need to work with our engineers and our residents to confirm our priorities, restart stalled initiatives, and identify and execute work that is in line with the priorities in that plan. With federal grants now drying up and our own tight budget, our options are limited, but we can still make meaningful progress.
How would you as an Oxford commissioner ease tensions between residents and the commission?
Rebuilding trust is essential, and it starts by electing new leadership that is not tied to and responsible for past mistakes. Much of our tension is due to poor communication by the commissioners. We need more open and candid discussions by the commissioners about matters that come before them so that residents can understand what the commissioners are thinking and why (and vice versa). Commissioners need to provide actual answers to questions that are asked. Too often, questions are acknowledged but never answered. With new leadership and better communication, we can rebuild the trust between our residents and the commissioners.
What is your vision for the Strand Beach project?
We must get this project behind us. We don't have the money to redesign or rebuild it, and it appears we waived many of our legal rights when the commissioners prematurely signed off on its completion last year. The only course now is to figure out what needs to be done to finish it, including restoring public and ADA access and minimizing the hazards created by the "natural" features in the islands. We should never again embark on a project of this magnitude just because we found a funding source, especially one for which there was no clear design at the outset.

title: Talbot Council, Planning Commission Weigh in on Controversial Short-Term Rental Restrictions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Planning Commission members are largely skeptical of proposals to increase regulations on short-term rentals in the county.During a joint workshop with the County Council on Tuesday, the commission reviewed legislation sponsored by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher. Planning Commission members said they struggled to understand why stricter rules for short-term rentals were necessary.
Commission Member Chip Councell said some of the proposed items are more of a "hindrance" than an improvement to the county's existing rules.
"I would almost support an easing of some of the restrictions more so than getting more stringent," Councell said. "I'm struggling to see this as a balance."
Mielke has previously said the legislation was drafted amid a "proliferation" of short-term rentals in Talbot County, noting her concerns for St. Michaels village communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista.
Mielke said Tuesday that in village zones, some communities don't have covenants or restrictions on the temporary rentals. County attorney Patrick Thomas, who helped draft the legislation, noted it can be "tricky" to change covenants since many require 75 to 80% of homeowners to agree.
"They can be overwhelmed by short-term rentals, so the idea was to sort of make a distinction," Mielke said.
Mielke added that an increasing number of short-term rentals are "being scooped up by investors," which she says is hurting the county's affordable housing stock. Planning Commission members disagreed.
"I don't see where this is a proliferation," Councell said, citing that the number of licensed short-term rentals hasn't significantly increased or reached 200 in the last few years.
"They're taking them from subpar to show pieces for people to come down and enjoy," said commission chair James Corson. " … I don't think the majority of these are even in that range of affordable housing."
Some of the new restrictions if the legislation is passed would include: mandatory landlines; more detailed stay logs for license renewals; a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts; and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
The proposals have drawn support from a number of residents around the county but sharp criticism from short-term rental property agents and owners who view them as government overreach.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license to operate a short-term rental. Most license requests are granted.
Corson raised qualms with how the proposed seven-night minimum stay could deter tourists from attending weekend events such as the Waterfowl Festival. Lesher acknowledged it's "largely a weekend business" and said he's comfortable keeping the current three-day minimum in place.
County Council member Dave Stepp weighed in against proposals for more detailed logs and required landlines.
"To have that legislation in there, it just doesn't make any sense," he said of the landlines.
No official changes were made to the draft regulations Tuesday. The commission will hold a public hearing and discuss the legislation at its July 2 meeting. A recommendation will then be made to the council, likely with significant revisions to the original proposals.
Planning Commission vice chair Michael Strannahan said the issue comes down to preserving the balance between economic benefits and maintaining the county's complexion.
"It's the old growth versus character thing we face all the time," Strannahan said.

Cambridge steps up code enforcement

 CAMBRIDGE — City Manager Glenn Steckman said Cambridge is stepping up its code enforcement as trash cans are increasingly left on the sidewalk, grass is going uncut and cars are parked in the wrong direction."There seems to be a lack of lawnmowers in our community because the grass and grass height has been an ongoing issue in the town, and we're having to send violation notices out," Steckman said.
Code enforcement is a process used by local governments to enforce state and local laws, codes or ordinances regarding housing, building and health standards. The city's stepped-up code enforcement efforts became a topic of discussion at the Cambridge City County's meeting Monday after a resident raised concerns and confusion.
Cambridge resident Sharon Wilson was fined $200 due to a partially knocked down brick wall on her property. Wilson presented images of the fallen wall to the City Council, saying she feels zoning codes are being enforced unfairly.
Wilson said a city staff member stopped by her property asking her to clean up the bricks.
"They told me I had to clean it up, and he said, 'You cleaned it, but you didn't clean it up enough.' OK, so what is enough for you?" Wilson said.
She continued to address the council asking if this is something they do for all city residents.
"I said that's a lie. You're not fair," Wilson said. "Because if you're being fair you'd be going to the city limits checking all the properties."
Wilson said she "was shocked" when she drove around the city to look at the properties and saw many that were "more of hazard" than hers.
"We want to make sure she understands that she is not being picked on," Steckman said. "That this is not just her issue, this is a Cambridge issue."
He said that the city has received a growing number of code-related complaints, which is why the city is sending out more citations than in previous years.
Steckman said the city has sent out a notice to residents outlining the city's code standards and plans to send another one soon.

title: Let's Be Neighbors, Smile More

Let's be neighbors, smile more

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox
