 Gosh, I miss Rick Kollinger. I can only imagine his spot on wit lampooning in cartoon form the downright laughable issue currently clogging the Talbot County political landscape that is "Short-Term Rentals." I envision an Eastern Shoreman standing bewildered in a sea of yard signs reading "Came Here's" vs. "Been Here's," "From 'Round Here's" vs. "Come Down Here's," all with directional arrows pointing every which way, a political compass gone rogue. The ol' bait and switch, alive and well.Folks, there is no issue of concern relating to STRs, not to be confused with STDs, but surprisingly similar in their effect on a community. Reminds me of a brief stint I spent in Florida, living in a community complex of all ages. There was a newsletter sharing the happenings of the neighborhood, a must-read. Almost monthly there was a "noise complaint" from Ms. Unhappy with the world. This went on for what seemed like forever. It turned out the plaintiff kept hearing kids playing in the pool. It disturbed her peaceful existence, I was told. I said to myself, what, for real? Then, the tables turned.
We had a good old-fashioned BBQ with most participating. A great time was being had. Lo and behold, a well-dressed lady arrived and eased into the crowd. It was soon obvious she was the one and only Ms. Unhappy. The crowd seemed off for a bit when a young girl ran over and gave a tug on her dress and handed her a brownie. We tried not to notice, but you couldn't help yourself. She then gave Ms. Unhappy a hug and the world changed in front of our eyes. Our neighbor of discontent smiled and said, "Thank you, darlin'." It took a few minutes to soak it all in, but I think she just wanted to, well, feel included. A simple random act of kindness by, god forbid, a child – go figure. It worked magic. No more noise complaint letters appeared in our cherished gossip monthly.
Moral of the story, give this a try: Let's be neighbors again, solve our own perceived problems, and smile a little more – "It makes people wonder what your thinkin' about." Leave the heavy lifting to our chosen political friends, they have a lot to do. And let's just make and share some brownies. Just be kind!
ROO WOOD
Easton

Mobile competition is beneficial

 I'm not clear why we differentiate between brick-and-mortar businesses and mobile businesses.As a previous owner of a brick-and-mortar business, I had mobile competitors. I took the approach that while I could offer a significantly larger array of products and services, there are customers that will opt for a less comprehensive menu.
I could have started a mobile service too, but the customer base I sought was not those needing or desiring limited mobile options.
So I would advise Easton council to treat mobile businesses like the brick-and-mortar ones. Charge them the same annual fee. Collect the taxes on their income. Collect taxes on the wages they pay their staff. And require the mobile businesses to adhere to the same OSHA, Department of Health, etc. laws and ordinances that all brick-and-mortar businesses are required to follow.
Restaurant owners aren't happy when another restaurant opens. Liquor stores aren't happy when another liquor store opens. But it's called competition.
Maybe … just maybe … mobile competition will get brick-and-mortar businesses to create competitive options rather than asking local governments to stifle them.

title: Federalsburg Activities Center Hopes to Bring Joy to the Whole Community
author: Ahmad Garnett
content:
Federalsburg Activities Center hopes to bring joy to the whole community

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 631

 FEDERALSBURG — An idea for a space where children could have fun in Federalsburg turned into a place where everyone could have fun.The Federalsburg Activities Center began with a conversation between the Rev. Pam Bockart and the Rev. Stanford Ricks at a meeting in 2019.
Bockart was the Pastor at Christ Church, and she recalled "kids outside just walking the streets having nowhere to go."
She decided to call a meeting about finding something for the children to do. After the meeting, Bockart and Ricks selected a location for a community center project at the old Dollar General building on Morris Avenue in Federalsburg.
Ricks is the vice president of Men for Change, an organization the specializes in "changing our community through service" by mentoring youth in Federalsburg. The group wanted a central location.
A partnership was formed. For the next five years, Bockart, Ricks and a board of stakeholders overcame financial and logistical obstacles to open the Federalsburg Activities Center.
"We started on a journey. We had nothing, no money, just a vision to open up this building," Ricks said, looking around the center, which opened in the former Dollar General building earlier this year.
The group gained ownership of the building with help from its former owner and a loan. But even after the building's ownership was squared away, multiple renovations needed to be done to make the space functional.
After multiple grants, donations from local businesses and an anonymous $400,000 private donation, the Activities Center was renovated and ready for the community.
"Over the five years, we never got frustrated," Ricks said. "That was the great thing to me. The the board that we had, we met every week, we came here, we enjoyed each other, we talked positive and never got frustrated. I think we kind of knew it was going to be a long journey.
"... So now we went from phase one, which was to get the building open. Now were going into phase two of the project, getting the programs up and running in the building."
The current programs at the Activities Center are Men For Change on Friday, bible study on Saturday, senior lunches on Friday, garden club once a month and Make Federalsburg Beautiful meetings once a month. Men For Change sees 30 to 50 kids on Fridays, and the senior lunches see 20 to 40 seniors.
Part of the next phase for the center will be partnering youth with older community members. Board members said older community members tend to feel left out, with a lack of activities catered toward them. The board hopes this partnership will increase seniors' drive and provide mentorship opportunities for local youth.
"We would like to bring the young ones, who are starting their vision, and the old ones, who have their vision, and we want them to kind of get together so that the seniors can tell the younger ones about their story and how to get there themselves that they may have a good life," Ricks said.
Another part of the next phase is adding new programs within the activities center. The board has plans to add a science, technology, engineering and mathematics program; arts and crafts; a coffee club; and a running club. Board members said negotiations for Boys and Girls Club and 4-H partnerships are ongoing.
The board is most excited about the potential of what the activities center can do for the town of Federalsburg.
"There is something in all of us when we give to others," said Wendy Garner, secretary for the board. "We get back as much if not more, and that's what I think all these skills, all these learning curves, whether it's for the kids, the adults, or the seniors — this is a community center."
The board encourages all community members who want volunteer or who have ideas to email fac2024@aol.com.
